There's a word I keep returning to: "petrichor"—the smell of rain on dry earth. What delights me isn't just the word itself, coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, but the fact that someone felt the need to name it at all. The smell existed for millennia before anyone bothered. People simply walked outside after a storm, breathed deeply, and felt something they couldn't articulate.

This gap fascinates me—the space between experience and language. So much of human life happens in that unnamed territory. The specific melancholy of Sunday evenings. The strange intimacy of seeing a coworker at the grocery store. The way a song you loved at sixteen can collapse a decade in three seconds. Some languages have caught a few of these: the Portuguese have "saudade," the Japanese have "mono no aware," the Germans seem to have a compound word for nearly everything. But most experiences remain wild and unlabeled, roaming around in our heads.

I sometimes wonder whether naming a feeling changes it. Once "petrichor" exists, do we smell rain differently? Perhaps naming domesticates experience—makes it shareable but also smaller, the way a photograph of a mountain is both a gift and a diminishment.

And yet I can't bring myself to mourn this. The act of reaching for words, even imperfect ones, is its own kind of pleasure. Every metaphor is a small bridge thrown across the gap. We never quite get to the other side, but the building itself—clumsy, hopeful, endless—might be the most human thing we do.
